lead: Both readings ask where true teaching and true faith come from. Hebrews looks back at the patriarchs, who trusted God's promise even when it seemed to lead to death: Abraham on the mountain with Isaac, Isaac and Jacob blessing sons they would not see grow old, Joseph speaking of an exodus that lay centuries ahead. In John, Jesus teaches in the temple at the feast of Booths and says that his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and that whoever is ready to do God's will shall recognise it. The key words are faith and right judgment.

r.h: By faith Abraham offered up Isaac
set: Hebrews 11 is the great roll of honour of faith. It opens with a definition: “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1), and then walks through the story of Israel, each example beginning with the same Greek word, pistei, “by faith”. Our verses come after the call of Abraham (11:8–16) and turn to the testing of his faith and to the blessings handed on by Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, all taken from Genesis 22 to 50.
str: vv. 17–19: Abraham offers Isaac, trusting that God can raise the dead.
v. 20: Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau.
v. 21: the dying Jacob blesses the sons of Joseph.
v. 22: the dying Joseph speaks of the exodus and gives orders about his bones.
kw: The word that begins each example of the chapter like a drum beat. Faith here is not a vague feeling. It is trust in God's word that shows itself in acts: leaving, offering, blessing, giving orders for a future one will not see.

The same word John uses of Christ, “the only Son” (John 3:16). Abraham had another son, Ishmael, but Isaac was the one son of the promise. The word prepares the Christian reader to see in Isaac a figure of the Father's only Son.
Literally “in a parable” or “as a figure”. Isaac did not die, but Abraham received him back as if from the dead, and this return was itself a sign pointing ahead.
vv: By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac.
The test of Genesis 22 seemed to set God's command against God's promise, since the promise was to come through Isaac. Abraham held on to both, trusting that God would not contradict himself.
He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead
Hebrews reads the story of Moriah in the light of Easter. Abraham's faith reached beyond death long before the resurrection was revealed.
By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, “bowing in worship over the top of his staff.”

The phrase about the staff comes from the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew text has “the head of his bed”. The two words differ only in their vowels, which were not written in ancient Hebrew.
By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his burial.

Joseph asked that his bones be carried up from Egypt (Genesis 50:24–25). Moses did so at the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). A dying man's faith looked some four hundred years ahead.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses when it speaks of Abraham's prayer and faith: asked to sacrifice the son God had given him, Abraham did not waver, for he considered that God was able to raise men even from the dead, and so the father of believers was conformed to the likeness of the Father who would not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). From the earliest centuries Christians have seen in Isaac, carrying the wood up the mountain, a figure of Christ carrying his cross, and in the ram offered in his place a sign of the Lamb whom God himself provides.

r.h: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me
set: Booths, or Tabernacles, was the joyful autumn pilgrimage feast, when people lived in shelters of branches to remember the wandering in the wilderness. Jesus had gone up to Jerusalem quietly, “not publicly but as it were in secret” (7:10). Now, half way through the week of the feast, he teaches openly in the temple.

The argument looks back to John 5, where Jesus healed a man at the pool of Bethesda on a sabbath and some of the authorities began to seek his death (5:16–18). In this Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, his mother and his disciples were all Jews, and “the crowd” in verse 20 does not know of any plot.
str: vv. 14–15: Jesus teaches; the hearers wonder at his learning.
vv. 16–18: his teaching comes from the one who sent him.
vv. 19–20: the law of Moses and the plot to kill him.
vv. 21–24: circumcision on the sabbath and the healing of a whole man: judge with right judgment.
kw: Literally “letters”. The question is how Jesus can teach the Scriptures so deeply when he has not studied under a recognised teacher. His answer points to the true source of his teaching: the Father.
Jesus does not deny that he teaches. He denies that the teaching is his own invention. The Son speaks what he receives from the Father, as a messenger speaks for the one who sends him.
A just verdict that looks at the truth of a matter and not at its surface. Isaiah says of the coming king that “he shall not judge by what his eyes see” (Isaiah 11:3).
vv: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.

St Augustine draws out the paradox: the teaching of the Son is the Word of the Father, and the Son is that Word; so nothing is more his own, and yet it is wholly the Father's (Tractates on John 29, in substance).
Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God

Knowledge of God is not reached only by argument. The one who is ready to obey comes to understand. Augustine puts it this way: understanding is the reward of faith (Tractates on John 29, in substance).
Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.

Jesus argues as the teachers of his day argued: if circumcision, which touches one part of the body, may be done on the sabbath, how much more may a whole man be healed? Later rabbis used a similar argument to allow saving a life on the sabbath.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, sent as a man to men, speaks the words of God and completes the work of salvation that the Father gave him to do (Dei Verbum 4). The Church therefore does not treat the Gospel as one opinion among many but receives it as the teaching of the Father given in the Son. Verse 17 is also a word of encouragement for every searcher: the honest will to do what God asks is already a door to faith.

qa: Did God really want Abraham to kill his son?

The story itself says that God was testing Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and God stops his hand. In a world where some peoples offered children to their gods, the story teaches the opposite: the God of Israel does not want human sacrifice, and he himself provides the offering. For Christians it points to the one sacrifice God did not withhold, the gift of his own Son, which no human father was asked to make.
study: The patriarchs blessed a future they would not see. What blessing am I handing on to the next generation in my family and parish?
Jesus says that whoever is ready to do God's will shall know his teaching. Is there something God is asking of me that I am delaying, and could that be why I find faith hard?
